summary: Nir Gazit opens with the provocative claim that prompt engineering is dead and never really existed, characterizing manual prompt crafting as merely asking LLMs to behave. He motivates the talk with a real problem: a simple RAG-based documentation chatbot on the Traceloop website that answered questions adequately but made too many mistakes. Rather than hand-tuning prompts, he envisioned an auto-improving machine that researches prompting techniques online, applies them, and iterates toward optimal performance. The system requires three components: a RAG pipeline, an evaluator, and an auto-improving agent. The RAG pipeline uses a Chroma vector database and OpenAI. For evaluation, Gazit chose LLM-as-judge over classic NLP metrics for ease of building and deployment, creating a ground-truth dataset of 20 questions with 3 expected facts each (60 total), yielding a numeric boolean-based score. The final component is a CrewAI researcher agent that takes an initial prompt, runs the evaluator, collects failure reasons, combines them with crawled prompting guides to generate an improved prompt, and loops. The initial score was 0.4; after two iterations it reached 0.9. In closing, Gazit frames this as running gradient ascent on the evaluator score, achievable either automatically with an agent or manually by studying prompting guides. He candidly acknowledges overfitting risk from using only 20 examples and recommends classic ML train/test splits. He also notes the meta-irony: he did substantial manual prompt engineering to build the optimizing agent itself, and speculates about having the agent optimize its own and the evaluator's prompts. The demo is available in the traceloop/autoprompting_demo repo.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Manual prompt engineering doesn't scale and can be replaced with a test-driven, iterative agent approach
An auto-improving prompt system requires three components: a RAG pipeline, an evaluator, and an agent that iterates on prompts
LLM-as-judge was chosen over classic NLP metrics for ease of building, deployment, and flexibility with or without ground truth
A ground-truth dataset of 20 questions with 3 expected facts each (60 total facts) provides a numeric boolean-based scoring mechanism
Starting from 0.4, two iterations improved the score to 0.9 (90% facts correct) with zero manual prompt engineering on the target prompt
Overfitting is a real risk with small datasets; classic ML train/test/eval splits are recommended to mitigate it
The approach resembles running gradient ascent on the evaluator score, either automatically via an agent or manually by studying prompting guides
The meta-problem remains: the agent and evaluator prompts themselves require manual engineering, suggesting possible recursive self-optimization

sections.title: Introduction: Prompt Engineering Is Dead
sections.summary: Gazit claims prompt engineering never truly existed as engineering, describing it as merely asking LLMs to behave. He introduces his goal of improving a simple RAG-based documentation chatbot on the Traceloop website without manual prompt tuning.

sections.title: Vision: Auto-Improving Prompt Machine
sections.summary: Gazit envisions an automated system with an agent that researches prompting techniques online and iteratively applies them. He outlines the three required components: RAG pipeline, evaluator, and auto-improving agent.

sections.title: RAG Pipeline Demo
sections.summary: Demonstrates the simple RAG pipeline using a Chroma database and OpenAI, showing how a question flows through vector retrieval and context-augmented generation to produce an answer.

sections.title: Evaluator Design and Setup
sections.summary: Discusses evaluator types (LLM-as-judge vs classic NLP metrics), why LLM-as-judge was chosen, and multiple evaluation levels. Details the ground-truth dataset of 20 questions with 3 expected facts each and the boolean pass/fail scoring mechanism.

sections.title: Evaluator Demo
sections.summary: Shows the evaluator running against the question dataset, invoking the RAG pipeline, checking answers against expected facts, and calculating a numeric score. Notes the process is slow.

sections.title: Agent Demo and Results
sections.summary: Demonstrates the CrewAI researcher agent crawling prompting guides, running evaluations, analyzing failure reasons, and regenerating improved prompts. Initial score of 0.4 reached 0.9 after two iterations.

sections.title: Closing Thoughts: Gradient Ascent, Overfitting, and Meta-Engineering
sections.summary: Gazit frames automated prompt optimization as running gradient ascent on the evaluator score. He candidly acknowledges overfitting risk from only 20 examples, recommending classic ML train/test/eval splits. He admits he still did substantial manual prompt engineering on the agent itself, noting the meta-irony, and speculates about recursive self-optimization. He shares the demo repo link (traceloop/autoprompting_demo) and invites questions.
